source.title: Sparse autoencoders find composed features in small toy models

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAEs recover known underlying features or composed features in a small synthetic toy setting. It does not test dictionary-size splitting, parent-child input partitioning, feature families, absorption, or decomposition between larger and smaller dictionaries.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes concern SAE recovery of composed versus designated underlying features, not splitting as dictionary size increases. No result tests the claim versions directly; the toy-model results are recorded under fits_no_version. No results are reported for p(one-hot)=0.5.
record.test_reason: The post trains fixed-size SAEs on a two-hidden-dimension toy model. It asks whether they recover designated 'true' features or composed pairs. It never varies dictionary size and never measures coarse-to-fine splitting, feature families, parent/child absorption, or decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE ones. The ℓ1-driven composition idea is close in spirit to V6, but V6 concerns splitting, which is not measured here. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that ℓ1 SAEs in this toy setting learn composed features rather than the designated ones, and that hyperparameter sweeps and cosine penalties don't robustly fix this. In comments, the author concedes the first dataset's actual features are the diagonal pairs, and that principal components explain the second dataset's results.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains SAEs on synthetic two-set, two-feature toy-model activations and compares recovered features with designated underlying features; it does not vary dictionary size or measure parent-child splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with feature-amplitude correlation, learning rate, λ, SAE realization, and inclusion of one-hot vectors; the cosine-term formulation also affects whether decoder vectors collapse.

fits_no_version.finding: In a two-hidden-dimension toy model with two sets of two anticorrelated features, lowest-loss ℓ1 SAEs mostly learn composed-pair directions rather than the designated features. This holds across learning rate and λ. The effect is cleaner with uncorrelated amplitudes and persists partly when 75% of inputs are one-hot. Commenters showed, and the author accepted, that the data's principal directions are the 45° diagonals, so the 'true' basis is questionable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small synthetic datasets, ℓ1 SAEs can recover composed or principal-direction features instead of the experimenter-designated feature basis.

fits_no_version.finding: Two decoder cosine-similarity penalties did not improve monosemantic recovery. The absolute-value version could collapse decoder vectors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoder orthogonality penalties do not fix composed-feature learning in this toy setting.

record.problems: The experiments use a highly simplified model with two hidden dimensions and only two sets of two features. The post focuses on uniform feature distributions and does not test the feature-frequency and correlation variations it identifies as future work. In the comments, the authors accept that the first dataset did not have the intended underlying feature basis; they also acknowledge that the second dataset's principal directions help explain the SAE results.

untested.parts: All: dictionary size is never varied.
All: only a two-dimensional toy model is used; no large models or open SAE releases.
All: no feature families or hierarchy geometry are examined.
All: no parent/child latent firing is measured; sparsity is varied, but only for composition, not absorption.
All: SAEs of different sizes are never compared.
Splitting itself and alternative objectives such as Matryoshka are not studied. The ℓ1-composition result bears on a related construct (see fits_no_version).

missing.what: Results for p(one-hot)=0.5 were run but not shown. The text only says SAEs are more likely to find true features than with no one-hot inputs.
missing.locator: What if the SAE Actually Gets to See the True Features?

record.verdict_notes: In a comment, the author mentions preliminary, unreported observations that larger dictionaries get stuck less in local minima. This is anecdotal, with no numbers, and cannot support a verdict on dictionary-size effects. The reader's T6/discusses classification is retained.

relation.reason: Post studies a related l1-objective failure mode (composed vs true features) without citing or testing feature splitting; discusses is the closest fit.

tranche.reason: Fixed-size SAEs on a 2-hidden-dimension toy model with composed (not hierarchical) features; never varies dictionary size, never mentions or measures splitting, families or absorption.

source_check.notes: Comments concede the first dataset's real features are the diagonal composed pairs (principal components 45 degrees off), weakening the 'composed features' result. The author says larger dictionaries preliminarily avoid the local minima, but gives no data; the cosine-term runs (r5, r6) don't state which C was used.
